digest.definition: The study of ancient Greece and Rome from the late Bronze Age to Late Antiquity, of Byzantium from 324 to 1453 CE and of the Greek-speaking world from the late medieval period on, widening to other ancient cultures and to reception in every period
distinctiveFeatures: The study of ancient Greece and Rome from the late Bronze Age to Late Antiquity, of Byzantium from 324 to 1453 CE and of the Greek-speaking world from the late medieval period on, widening to other ancient cultures and to reception in every period
Interdisciplinary by nature: art, archaeology, history, language and linguistics, literature, philology, philosophy, law, science, medicine and reception, studied in varying mixes

Several routes into the classical: Classics with both ancient languages, single-language Greek or Latin, Classical Studies, Ancient History, Classical Archaeology, Modern Greek and Late Antique and Byzantine Studies
Languages are central but not universal: Classics and Modern Greek require proficiency, other routes offer languages at several entry points
Critical handling of fragmentary, varied evidence, material, written and digital, is its characteristic method
It sees Greek and Roman societies as linked with each other and with the wider Mediterranean and beyond, through influence, conflict and borrowing
A self-critical discipline: it confronts its reputation for elitism and its ties to empire, colonialism, race and class
A liberal, non-vocational tradition that nonetheless builds a broad platform of transferable skills valued by employers

themesInSubject.inThisSubject: the subject confronts its elitist reputation and its links with imperialism, colonialism, white supremacy and class; it calls for inclusive curricula, diverse reading lists, decolonising approaches, inclusive peer groups and care with sensitive topics such as slavery (D1, 1.22 to 1.25, 2.4, 3.4, 3.14)

headed Accessibility in the text: students arrive by varied routes, including popular culture and online platforms; blended and online delivery, captioning and recording, low-risk options, language pathways and adjustments for fieldwork and assessment (D1, 2.1 to 2.3, 2.9, 2.10, 3.16, 3.21, 3.22)

headed Sustainability in the text: dialogue with antiquity puts modern values such as growth and consumerism in perspective; ancient evidence bears on four UN goals; the subject builds four UNESCO competences: systems thinking, critical thinking, collaboration and integrated problem-solving (D1, 1.26 to 1.29)

headed Entrepreneurship and enterprise education, with employability: not labelled as such but built into the curriculum through problem-solving, creative thinking and project-based assessment; careers advice, placements and work schemes (D1, 1.17, 1.18, 1.30, 1.31, 2.12)

subjectSpecific.text: You will understand another culture, through its writing, ideas, history or objects, think critically about it and see how it compares with cultures today.
You will build a broad, joined-up knowledge of several related fields, such as languages, literature, philosophy, history or archaeology, or of themes like gender or religion that run across them.
You will get to know a wide range of original sources, from texts of many kinds to objects, archaeological finds, inscriptions and papyri.

You will learn to use a range of the subject's methods, such as library research, close reading, handling fragmentary evidence, databases and digital tools, visual analysis, statistics, argument and translation.
You will understand different views on how to interpret and judge evidence, and be able to use several critical approaches from across the subject.
You will become independent enough to research a classical topic yourself, build a clear argument and present it well in speech and in writing.
You will gain an analytical command of at least one ancient or modern language: its grammar, vocabulary, idioms, tone and translation, with speaking and listening where the language allows.

transferable.text: You will become largely self-directed, taking the lead in your own learning and managing your study time.
You will be able to look critically at what you have learned and how, including where your understanding stops.
You will be able to reach critical judgements based on evidence and argument.
You will be able to be creative in how you develop ideas and arguments and how you share them.
You will learn to understand and feel for people whose lives differ from yours, using the ancient world as a way of seeing them.
You will understand today's issues more deeply by seeing their long and complex history.
You will be open to working across subjects, drawing on varied ideas and trying new methods.
You will be able to collect, remember, organise and use evidence and see what it means when evidence is missing.
You will be able to pick out what matters in complex information and spot and solve the problems it raises.
You will be able to choose and use the right methods to work out what information means and why it matters.
You will be able to analyse and weigh up texts, evidence and arguments, decide for yourself what is relevant, choose between competing theories and reach your own judgements.
You will be able to judge critically how useful digital resources are for studying the ancient world, and how they shape what you find.
You will be able to think sideways, making creative links between ideas from different fields.
You will be able to put arguments together clearly, coherently and concisely, in speech and in writing.
You will be able to appreciate and judge literature, art and other written and material evidence critically.
You will be able to give a clear, effective talk, using visual or audio aids where they help, shaped for your audience, with adjustments where needed.
You will be able to write clearly and with care, reference sources properly and lay out your work well, with tables, diagrams or images where they help.
You will be able to work creatively and adapt, both on your own and with other people.
You will be able to organise your own work, study on your own, write and think under pressure and hit deadlines.

You will be able to use digital tools well at every stage of your work: finding and judging digital data, using online texts and databases, presenting your work digitally and keeping safe and secure online.
You will be able to read many kinds of sources critically, ask where they come from and pull them together without taking anything on trust.
You will be able to work in a range of settings, through placements with organisations such as museums, galleries, charities, archaeology firms, libraries or archives.

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Classics and Ancient History (including Byzantine Studies and Modern Greek) degree

statements.appliesTo: the subject, its departments and the education universities provide
statements.about: facing the subject's history of elitism, empire and race
statements.paraphrase: Classics and its neighbouring fields have long been seen as elitist and exclusive, a reputation that persists despite recent work to widen who studies and teaches them and to broaden their scope. The subject must now confront and account for its own past: its ties, positive and negative, to empire, colonial rule, white supremacy and class are a part of university teaching that cannot be avoided, whether assessed or discussed.

forPractitioner.text: Treat the subject's own history as course content you must address: its connections with empire, colonialism, racial supremacy and class, good and bad. Decide where this is assessed and where it is opened up for discussion, so that no student leaves without meeting it.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the subject and its teachers; the student meets its effect through the curriculum

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Classics and Ancient History (including Byzantine Studies and Modern Greek) degree

statements.appliesTo: teaching and curriculum in the subject
statements.about: inclusive curriculum and teaching against elitism
statements.paraphrase: Elitism can show in both the content and the manner of teaching, so work remains to open the subject to wider audiences and make teaching more inclusive: curriculum material that serves students new to the subject and that features under-represented groups in core teaching. Teaching can show that the subject's methods use antiquity to explore lasting issues; the ethics of these topics and students' intersecting identities need to be acknowledged and addressed, especially by linking antiquity with the present.

forPractitioner.text: Design curriculum material for students meeting the subject for the first time and bring under-represented groups into core teaching. Show that the methods of the subject use antiquity to look at enduring questions, and make room to acknowledge the ethics of the topics and the ways students' social, economic or political identities may expose them to discrimination.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the teaching and curriculum; the student meets its effect

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Classics and Ancient History (including Byzantine Studies and Modern Greek) degree

statements.appliesTo: learning opportunities in the subject
statements.about: equal access by inclusive design and individual adjustments
statements.paraphrase: An inclusive learning environment plans ahead for learners' varied needs and aims for equal access to education; students should be offered opportunities that all can reach, through inclusive design wherever it is possible and reasonable individual adjustments where they are needed.

forPractitioner.text: Design learning so that everyone can reach it from the start, and add reasonable individual adjustments only where inclusive design falls short; plan for varied needs rather than reacting to them.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course to offer accessible learning; the student meets its effect

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Classics and Ancient History (including Byzantine Studies and Modern Greek) degree

statements.appliesTo: courses and student-led study groups
statements.about: progression from any starting point; inclusive student-led groups
statements.paraphrase: Courses support progress whatever a student's starting point, built on the distance from entry to the attributes of an honours graduate: core modules carry what the award needs, options follow interests, language teaching comes at several levels where possible, and skills training helps students judge their own skills; peer mentoring and group study help students learn together, and care should be taken that student-led groups include everyone.

forPractitioner.text: Plan the course around how far each student must travel from entry to graduation: core modules for what the award needs, options for interests, staged language teaching where you can and skills training with honest feedback on skill levels. Where you run peer mentoring or student-led groups, make sure they are inclusive.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a design duty on the course, with care for inclusive peer groups; the student meets its effect

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Classics and Ancient History (including Byzantine Studies and Modern Greek) degree

statements.appliesTo: students on an honours degree in the subject
statements.about: progress year by year towards the threshold and readiness for postgraduate study
statements.paraphrase: Across an honours degree at FHEQ level 6 (FQHEIS level 10), a student will progress from year to year under each institution's rules; each year is expected to build knowledge, expertise and experience towards meeting the threshold subject-specific and generic skills, and a graduate is expected to be able and prepared to start postgraduate study in the subject or a related one.

forPractitioner.text: Plan each year so that it adds knowledge, expertise and experience towards the threshold skills in section 4, and so that graduates are ready to begin postgraduate study in classics, ancient history or a neighbouring discipline.

forBeneficiary.text: Each year of your course will build towards the minimum skills an honours degree in the subject asks for, and by the end you are expected to be ready to go on to postgraduate study in this field or a related one if you choose.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Classics and Ancient History (including Byzantine Studies and Modern Greek) degree

statements.appliesTo: joint honours students in the subject
statements.about: joint honours reach the core skills and add others
statements.paraphrase: Joint honours students will reach the core of the subject's specific and generic skills and will add others from their second subject, and may also work in the overlap between the two for further interdisciplinary study.

forPractitioner.text: For joint honours, plan for students to reach the core specific and generic skills of this subject, to gain others from the partner subject and, where you can, to work across the two.

forBeneficiary.text: If you take this subject jointly with another, you will reach its core skills, gain others from your second subject and may get the chance to explore where the two meet.

statements.appliesTo: teaching in the subject
statements.about: teaching sensitive and challenging topics
statements.paraphrase: The subject can bring students into contact with sensitive or difficult topics, such as slavery and violence against particular groups, which may weigh most on marginalised students who have lived through such things; teaching should recognise the issues the material raises and allow for how students may react.

forPractitioner.text: When you teach topics such as slavery or violence against groups, name the issues the material raises, expect that some students, above all those from marginalised groups with lived experience, may react strongly, and plan for that in how you teach.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on teaching; the student meets its effect

statements.appliesTo: students on courses titled Classics
statements.about: proficiency in both ancient Greek and Latin on a Classics course
statements.paraphrase: A course called Classics generally requires its students to gain and show proficiency in both ancient Greek and Latin, and may make Greek and Latin literature the main though not the only focus, at least early on.

forPractitioner.text: If the course is titled Classics, require students to become proficient in both ancient Greek and Latin and to show it; you may centre the early years on the two literatures without making them the only focus.

forBeneficiary.text: On a course called Classics you will be required to learn both ancient Greek and Latin and to show that you can use them well.

statements.appliesTo: students on Modern Greek courses
statements.about: proficiency in the modern Greek language
statements.paraphrase: Modern Greek courses require proficiency in the modern language and centre on the writing, ideas, language and past of the Greek-speaking world from the later Middle Ages onwards.

forPractitioner.text: Build the course so that students become proficient in modern Greek and study the language, writing, ideas and past of the Greek-speaking world since the late medieval period.

forBeneficiary.text: On a Modern Greek course you will be required to become proficient in the language, and you will study the writing, ideas and history of the Greek-speaking world from the later Middle Ages to now.

headingPath: Examples of different modes of teaching and learning

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates and the courses they take
statements.about: the range of teaching and learning modes a graduate meets
statements.paraphrase: An honours graduate in the subject will usually have had the chance to meet all or most of a listed range of teaching and learning modes, from essays, language and source exercises, seminars and lectures to group projects, placements, field and museum work, digital production, examinations and a dissertation.

forPractitioner.text: Offer most of the listed modes across the course: essays, source, commentary and translation exercises, digital tools, seminars and lectures, one-to-one contact, group projects, work-based learning, reports, media analysis, work with objects in the field or museums, podcasts and blogs, exam revision and a dissertation.

forBeneficiary.text: Over your course you will usually get the chance to try most of these ways of learning: essays, translation and source exercises, seminars, lectures, group projects, placements, work with objects, podcasts or blogs, exams and a dissertation.

statements.appliesTo: courses offering ancient and later languages
statements.about: language learning at any stage through language pathways
statements.paraphrase: Where possible, students who want to should get the chance and encouragement to learn or improve Greek, Latin or another ancient Mediterranean language at any point in the degree. Unequal access before university calls for several language pathways and, where fitting, support towards comparable attainment by graduation, and arrangements should let students start language modules later in the course. Such study helps other skills and is a base for research degrees and an asset for master's study.

forPractitioner.text: Run more than one language pathway so that students with and without prior study can reach comparable attainment, give support where needed, and arrange things so that a student can begin or resume a language module later in the course, not only in the first year.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course to offer language pathways; the student meets its effect

headingPath: Example 2: classical or Byzantine art or field archaeology

statements.appliesTo: art, field archaeology and museum training in the subject
statements.about: training with objects and sites, with adjustments
statements.paraphrase: Training in Greek, Roman or Byzantine art, in fieldwork or in museum-based study of artefacts adds further skills; students may start it early or, where that was not possible, be offered it near the end of the course, and museum, gallery or field placements may be made available. Direct work with landscapes and objects builds skills for many jobs, and reasonable adjustments will be made for any such activity.

forPractitioner.text: Where you offer art, field or museum training, consider a late entry point for students who missed it, open placements where you can, and make reasonable adjustments for every such activity, from site surveys to drawing and recording.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course to make adjustments for practical training; the student meets its effect

statements.about: wide understanding of another culture and cultural difference
statements.paraphrase: Understands many features of a culture other than their own and is alert to cultural difference.

forPractitioner.text: At excellent level, graduates understand a wide range of a culture's features and show sensitivity to cultural difference.

forBeneficiary.text: For a first-class result you show that you understand a wide range of features of another culture and are alert to how cultures differ.

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in the subject (first class)
statements.about: a wide, diverse set of sources and deep understanding of combining evidence
statements.paraphrase: Is familiar with a wide, varied set of written and material sources and understands deeply how to use them with other evidence.

forPractitioner.text: At excellent level, graduates know a wide and diverse set of sources and understand in depth how to combine them with other evidence.

forBeneficiary.text: For a first-class result you know a wide and varied set of written sources and objects and understand in depth how to use them with other evidence.

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in the subject (first class)
statements.about: complex viewpoints and a wide variety of critical approaches
statements.paraphrase: Understands a broad range of sometimes complex positions on interpretation and evaluation and uses a wide variety of critical approaches.

forPractitioner.text: At excellent level, graduates understand a broad, sometimes complex range of positions and adopt a wide variety of critical approaches.

forBeneficiary.text: For a first-class result you understand a broad range of views, some of them complex, and use a wide variety of critical approaches.

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in the subject (first class)
statements.about: excellent research with cogent, nuanced argument
statements.paraphrase: Researches to an excellent standard, builds cogent and nuanced arguments and presents them lucidly in speech and writing.

forPractitioner.text: At excellent level, graduates research excellently, form cogent and nuanced arguments and present them lucidly orally and in writing.

forBeneficiary.text: For a first-class result you research to an excellent standard, build convincing and subtle arguments and present them clearly in speech and writing.

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in the subject (first class)
statements.about: high-standard thinking with sound and sometimes original judgement
statements.paraphrase: Thinks observantly, analytically and evaluatively to a high standard about evidence, arguments and readings, reaching sound and at times original judgements.

forPractitioner.text: At excellent level, graduates analyse and evaluate to a high standard and form sound, sometimes original judgements.

forBeneficiary.text: For a first-class result you analyse and weigh up evidence and arguments to a high standard and reach sound, sometimes original judgements.

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in the subject (first class)
statements.about: written presentation to a high standard
statements.paraphrase: Presents written material to a high standard, with discerning, lucid language, professional referencing and clear, effective layout.

forPractitioner.text: At excellent level, graduates present written work to a high standard with discerning, lucid language, professional referencing and clear layout.

forBeneficiary.text: For a first-class result your written work is presented to a high standard, with clear, careful language, professional references and a clear layout.

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in the subject (first class)
statements.about: key points and nuance from complex information; problems solved with a wide range of methods
statements.paraphrase: Draws both key points and nuance from complex information and recognises and solves the problems it raises with a wide range of methods.

forPractitioner.text: At excellent level, graduates extract key elements and nuance from complex information and solve problems with a wide range of methodologies.

forBeneficiary.text: For a first-class result you pick out both what matters and the finer points in complex information and solve problems using a wide range of methods.

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in the subject (first class)
statements.about: creativity and originality in problem-solving and communicating ideas
statements.paraphrase: Shows creativity and originality in solving problems and in developing and communicating ideas and arguments.

forPractitioner.text: At excellent level, graduates display creativity and originality in problem-solving and in developing and communicating ideas.

forBeneficiary.text: For a first-class result you show creativity and originality in solving problems and in developing and sharing ideas.

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in the subject (first class)
statements.about: considerable independence, effective time management and reflection
statements.paraphrase: Works with considerable independence and initiative, manages time well so tasks are finished on time, and reflects on progress.

forPractitioner.text: At excellent level, graduates work with considerable independence and initiative, manage time effectively and reflect on progress.

forBeneficiary.text: For a first-class result you work with real independence and initiative, manage your time well and reflect on your progress.

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in the subject (first class)
statements.about: creative, flexible group work
statements.paraphrase: Works creatively and adaptably with others on set group tasks.

forPractitioner.text: At excellent level, graduates work creatively and flexibly with others on assigned group tasks.

forBeneficiary.text: For a first-class result you work creatively and adaptably with others on group tasks.

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in the subject (first class)
statements.about: respect for others' views with enhanced critical reflection
statements.paraphrase: Respects other people's views and has a stronger capacity to reflect critically and change position when justified.

forPractitioner.text: At excellent level, graduates respect others' views with an enhanced capacity to reflect critically and modify their position.

forBeneficiary.text: For a first-class result you respect other people's views and are especially able to think critically about them and change your mind for good reason.

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in the subject (first class)
statements.about: effective and suitable use of digital resources and IT
statements.paraphrase: Uses digital resources and IT effectively and suitably to find information, communicate and support learning.

forPractitioner.text: At excellent level, graduates use digital resources and IT effectively and fittingly for information, communication and learning.

forBeneficiary.text: For a first-class result you use digital resources and technology well to find information, communicate and support your learning.
